questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about god's covenant with man?
questions.reference_answer: The distance between God and the creature is so great that although reasonable creatures do owe obedience unto him as their Creator, yet they could never have any fruition of him as their blessedness and reward but by some voluntary condescension on God's part, which he hath been pleased to express by way of covenant. The first covenant made with man was a covenant of works, wherein life was promised to Adam, and in him to his posterity, upon condition of perfect and personal obedience. Man by his fall having made himself incapable of life by that covenant, the Lord was pleased to make a second, commonly called the covenant of grace: wherein he freely offered unto sinners life and salvation by Jesus Christ, requiring of them faith in him that they may be saved, and promising to give unto all those that are ordained unto life his Holy Spirit, to make them willing and able to believe. This covenant of grace is frequently set forth in the Scripture by the name of a testament, in reference to the death of Jesus Christ the testator, and to the everlasting inheritance, with all things belonging to it, therein bequeathed. This covenant was differently administered in the time of the law and in the time of the gospel: under the law it was administered by promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the paschal lamb, and other types and ordinances delivered to the people of the Jews, all fore-signifying Christ to come, which were for that time sufficient and efficacious, through the operation of the Spirit, to instruct and build up the elect in faith in the promised Messiah, by whom they had full remission of sins and eternal salvation; and is called the Old Testament. Under the gospel, when Christ the substance was exhibited, the ordinances in which this covenant is dispensed are the preaching of the Word and the administration of the sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper; which, though fewer in number, and administered with more simplicity and less outward glory, yet in them it is held forth in more fulness, evidence, and spiritual efficacy, to all nations, both Jews and Gentiles; and is called the New Testament. There are not, therefore, two covenants of grace differing in substance, but one and the same under various dispensations.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) addresses God's covenant with man primarily in **Chapter 7**, titled "Of God's Covenant with Man." Here is a summary of its teaching:

## The Need for a Covenant

The Confession begins by noting the vast distance between God and man. Although humans owe obedience to God as their Creator, they could never have attained any reward or blessedness from Him except by God's voluntary condescension, which He expressed by way of covenant (WCF 7.1).

## Two Covenants

The Confession teaches that God has made **two covenants** with man:

### 1. The Covenant of Works (7.2)
- Made with Adam as a representative of all his posterity
- Promised life upon condition of perfect and personal obedience
- Adam's fall rendered humanity incapable of life by this covenant

### 2. The Covenant of Grace (7.3)
- Established because man made himself incapable of life by the first covenant
- God freely offers sinners life and salvation through Jesus Christ
- Requires faith in Christ to be saved
- God promises to give His Holy Spirit to the elect to make them willing and able to believe

## One Covenant of Grace, Two Administrations

A key Reformed distinctive emphasized in WCF 7.5-6 is that the covenant of grace was administered differently under the Old and New Testaments, but it is **substantially the same covenant**:

- **Under the Law (Old Testament):** Administered through promises, prophecies, sacrifices, circumcision, the paschal lamb, and other types and ordinances pointing forward to Christ
- **Under the Gospel (New Testament):** Administered through the preaching of the Word and the sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper, with greater simplicity, clarity, and spiritual efficacy

The Confession states: "There are not therefore two covenants of grace, differing in substance, but one and the same, under various dispensations" (7.6).

## Christ as Mediator

Chapter 8 follows by explaining that Jesus Christ is the Mediator of the covenant of grace—the prophet, priest, and king who fulfills the covenant on behalf of His people.

## Theological Significance

This covenantal framework is foundational to **Reformed covenant theology**, shaping how the Confession understands:
- The unity of Scripture (Old and New Testaments)
- Salvation by grace through faith in all ages
- The continuity between Israel and the Church
- The sacraments as covenant signs and seals

Would you like me to elaborate on any particular aspect of this covenantal teaching?

questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about christ the mediator?
questions.reference_answer: It pleased God, in his eternal purpose, to choose and ordain the Lord Jesus, his only-begotten Son, to be the Mediator between God and man, the Prophet, Priest, and King; the Head and Saviour of his Church, the Heir of all things, and Judge of the world; unto whom he did, from all eternity, give a people to be his seed, and to be by him in time redeemed, called, justified, sanctified, and glorified. The Son of God, the second person in the Trinity, being very and eternal God, of one substance, and equal with the Father, did, when the fulness of time was come, take upon him man's nature, with all the essential properties and common infirmities thereof, yet without sin: being conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost in the womb of the Virgin Mary, of her substance. So that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, the Godhead and the manhood, were inseparably joined together in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion. Which person is very God and very man, yet one Christ, the only mediator between God and man. The Lord Jesus, in his human nature thus united to the divine, was sanctified and anointed with the Holy Spirit above measure; having in him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, in whom it pleased the Father that all fulness should dwell; to the end that, being holy, harmless, undefiled, and full of grace and truth, he might be thoroughly furnished to execute the office of a mediator and surety. Which office he took not unto himself, but was thereunto called by his Father, who put all power and judgment into his hand, and gave him commandment to execute the same. This office the Lord Jesus did most willingly undertake, which, that he might discharge, he was made under the law, and did perfectly fulfill it; endured most grievous torments immediately in his soul, and most painful sufferings in his body; was crucified, and died; was buried, and remained under the power of death, yet saw no corruption. On the third day he arose from the dead, with the same body in which he suffered; with which also he ascended into heaven, and there sitteth at the right hand of his Father, making intercession; and shall return to judge men and angels at the end of the world. The Lord Jesus, by his perfect obedience and sacrifice of himself, which he through the eternal Spirit once offered up unto God, hath fully satisfied the justice of his Father, and purchased not only reconciliation, but an everlasting inheritance in the kingdom of heaven, for all those whom the Father hath given unto him. Although the work of redemption was not actually wrought by Christ till after his incarnation, yet the virtue, efficacy, and benefits thereof were communicated unto the elect, in all ages successively from the beginning of the world, in and by those promises, types, and sacrifices, wherein he was revealed, and signified to be the seed of the woman which should bruise the serpent's head, and the Lamb slain from the beginning of the world, being yesterday and today the same, and forever. Christ, in the work of mediation, acteth according to both natures; by each nature doing that which is proper to itself; yet, by reason of the unity of the person, that which is proper to one nature is sometimes, in Scripture, attributed to the person denominated by the other nature. To all those for whom Christ hath purchased redemption he doth certainly and effectually apply and communicate the same; making intercession for them, and revealing unto them, in and by the Word, the mysteries of salvation; effectually persuading them by his Spirit to believe and obey; and governing their hearts by his Word and Spirit; overcoming all their enemies by his almighty power and wisdom, in such manner and ways as are most consonant to his wonderful and unsearchable dispensation.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith addresses Christ as Mediator primarily in **Chapter VIII, "Of Christ the Mediator."** Here is a summary of its main teachings:

## Key Teachings

**1. Christ's Appointment as Mediator (8.1)**
God was pleased, in His eternal purpose, to choose and ordain the Lord Jesus, His only begotten Son, to be the Mediator between God and man. He was appointed to be Prophet, Priest, and King; Head and Savior of the Church; Heir of all things; and Judge of the world. God gave Him a people to be His seed, to be by Him in time redeemed, called, justified, sanctified, and glorified.

**2. The Two Natures of Christ (8.2)**
The Son of God, the second Person of the Trinity, being very and eternal God, of one substance with the Father, took upon Himself man's nature, with all its essential properties and common infirmities (yet without sin). He was conceived by the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary. Two whole, perfect, and distinct natures—divine and human—were inseparably joined in one Person, without conversion, composition, or confusion. This Person is truly God and truly man, yet one Christ, the only Mediator between God and man.

**3. Christ's Qualifications for Mediation (8.3)**
The Lord Jesus, in His human nature united to the divine, was sanctified and anointed with the Holy Spirit beyond measure, having all treasures of wisdom and knowledge. He was called by the Father to the office of Mediator and willingly undertook it.

**4. Christ's Humiliation and Exaltation (8.4)**
Christ willingly undertook this office, was made under the law, fulfilled it perfectly, endured grievous torments in His soul and painful sufferings in His body, was crucified and died, was buried, rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father, where He makes intercession and shall return to judge.

**5. Christ's Satisfaction and Purchase (8.5)**
By His perfect obedience and sacrifice of Himself, Christ fully satisfied the justice of His Father and purchased reconciliation and an everlasting inheritance for all those whom the Father has given Him.

**6. The Efficacy of Christ's Work Across Time (8.6)**
Although the work of redemption was not actually wrought by Christ until after His incarnation, its virtue, efficacy, and benefits were communicated to the elect in all ages from the beginning of the world.

**7. The Communication of Properties (8.7)**
Christ, in His work of mediation, acts according to both natures, by each nature doing what is proper to itself. Yet, because of the unity of the Person, what is proper to one nature is sometimes attributed in Scripture to the Person denominated by the other nature.

**8. Effectual Application of Redemption (8.8)**
To all those for whom Christ purchased redemption, He certainly and effectually applies and communicates the same. He makes intercession for them, reveals the mysteries of salvation to them in the Word, persuades them by His Spirit to believe and obey, and governs their hearts by His Word and Spirit—overcoming all their enemies by His almighty power and wisdom.

## Significance

This chapter is central to Reformed theology because it:
- Affirms the **unique mediatorship of Christ** (against any other mediators)
- Upholds **classical Christology** (true God, true man, in one Person)
- Teaches the **threefold office** (Prophet, Priest, King)
- Implies the doctrine of **definite/particular atonement** (especially in 8.5 and 8.8)
- Connects Christ's work to **covenant theology** and the **eternal decree** of God

questions.question: What does the Westminster Confession of Faith teach about effectual calling?
questions.reference_answer: All those whom God hath predestinated unto life, and those only, he is pleased, in his appointed and accepted time, effectually to call, by his Word and Spirit, out of that state of sin and death, in which they are by nature, to grace and salvation by Jesus Christ; enlightening their minds, spiritually and savingly, to understand the things of God; taking away their heart of stone, and giving unto them an heart of flesh; renewing their wills, and by his almighty power determining them to that which is good, and effectually drawing them to Jesus Christ; yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by his grace. This effectual call is of God's free and special grace alone, not from anything at all foreseen in man; who is altogether passive therein, until, being quickened and renewed by the Holy Spirit, he is thereby enabled to answer this call, and to embrace the grace offered and conveyed in it. The Westminster Confession of Faith addresses effectual calling primarily in Chapter 10. Here is a summary of its teaching:

## Core Definition

Effectual calling is the work by which God, at his appointed time, calls those whom he has predestined to life out of their natural state of sin and death into grace and salvation through Jesus Christ.

## Key Elements of the Doctrine

**1. The Source and Agents**
- It is God's work, accomplished "by His Word and Spirit"
- It flows from God's predestinating love, not from anything foreseen in the person

**2. What God Does in Effectual Calling**
According to WCF 10.1, God:
- Enlightens their minds spiritually to understand the things of God
- Takes away their heart of stone and gives them a heart of flesh
- Renews their wills
- Determines (by His almighty power) them to what is good
- Effectually draws them to Jesus Christ

**3. The Nature of the Response**
Though drawn effectually, those called "come most freely, being made willing by His grace" (10.1). This preserves both divine sovereignty and human willingness.

**4. Monergistic Grace**
WCF 10.2 emphasizes that this calling is:
- "Of God's free and special grace alone"
- "Not from anything at all foreseen in man"
- The person is "altogether passive therein, until, being quickened and renewed by the Holy Spirit"

**5. Special Cases (10.3)**
The Confession addresses elect infants dying in infancy and others incapable of being outwardly called by the ministry of the Word—they are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit who "worketh when, and where, and how He pleaseth."

**6. The Unconverted (10.4)**
Those not elected, even if called by the ministry of the Word and experiencing some common operations of the Spirit, cannot be saved apart from this effectual calling—nor can anyone be saved by other means, however diligent in framing their lives according to natural light.

## Theological Significance

This chapter sits between the chapters on free will (9) and justification (11), showing that effectual calling is the moment when God's eternal decree of election becomes actualized in time in the believer's experience, making salvation possible through faith.

The Westminster Shorter Catechism (Q. 31) gives a concise summary: "Effectual calling is the work of God's Spirit, whereby, convincing us of our sin and misery, enlightening our minds in the knowledge of Christ, and renewing our wills, he doth persuade and enable us to embrace Jesus Christ, freely offered to us in the gospel."

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) addresses justification primarily in Chapter 11. Its key teachings include:

## Core Doctrine

**Justification is a forensic (legal) act of God**, not a process of being made righteous. God declares sinners righteous rather than infusing righteousness into them. The Confession states God justifies the elect "not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous."

## Basis of Justification

The ground is **the imputed righteousness of Christ**—both his active obedience (fulfilling the law) and passive obedience (suffering the law's penalty). It is "not for any thing wrought in them, or done by them," but Christ's righteousness credited to believers.

## Means of Reception

**Faith alone** is the instrument of justification. However, the Confession carefully clarifies that this faith "is not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving graces, and is no dead faith, but worketh by love." Faith itself is not the righteousness that justifies—it is merely the instrument that receives Christ.

## Role of Christ

Christ's obedience and death **fully discharged the debt** of all who are justified and made "a proper, real, and full satisfaction to His Father's justice." Justification thus flows from God's free grace and Christ's exact justice simultaneously.

## God's Eternal Plan

God decreed from eternity to justify the elect, and Christ died for their sins in due time. However, they are "not justified, until the Holy Spirit doth, in due time, actually apply Christ unto them."

## Justification and Sin

Justified persons can fall under God's "fatherly displeasure" through sin and may need to renew their faith and repentance to restore the light of God's countenance—but they cannot fall from their state of justification.

## Old Testament Believers

Justification under the Old Covenant was the same in substance as under the New—through faith in the coming Messiah.

The Confession reflects classical Reformed orthodoxy, deliberately distinguishing its position from Roman Catholic (infused righteousness), Socinian, and Arminian views prevalent in the 17th century.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith addresses the perseverance of the saints primarily in Chapter 17, titled "Of the Perseverance of the Saints." Here is a summary of its teaching:

## Core Doctrine

**Chapter 17.1** states that those whom God has accepted in Christ, effectually called, and sanctified by His Spirit "can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace, but shall certainly persevere therein to the end, and be eternally saved."

## Basis of Perseverance

**Chapter 17.2** grounds perseverance not in the believer's own free will, but in:
- The immutability of God's decree of election, flowing from His free and unchangeable love
- The efficacy of the merit and intercession of Jesus Christ
- The abiding of the Spirit and seed of God within them
- The nature of the covenant of grace

From this arises both the certainty and infallibility of perseverance.

## Acknowledgment of Sin and Backsliding

**Chapter 17.3** offers a realistic view, acknowledging that true believers may:
- Fall into grievous sins through temptations of Satan and the world, the prevalence of corruption, and neglect of the means of preservation
- Continue in such sins for a time
- Incur God's displeasure
- Grieve the Holy Spirit
- Lose some measure of their graces and comforts
- Have their hearts hardened and consciences wounded
- Hurt and scandalize others
- Bring temporal judgments upon themselves

## Key Distinctions

The Confession carefully distinguishes between:
- **Falling into sin** (possible for believers) vs. **falling from grace** (impossible)
- **Loss of assurance or comfort** vs. **loss of salvation itself**

This doctrine is closely tied to other chapters, particularly Chapter 11 (Justification), Chapter 18 (Assurance of Grace and Salvation), and the broader covenantal framework of the Confession.

The teaching reflects classical Reformed soteriology, distinguishing it from Arminian views that allow for the possibility of final apostasy of true believers.

questions.response:
The Westminster Confession of Faith addresses the last judgment primarily in **Chapter 33, "Of the Last Judgment."** Here is a summary of its teaching:

## Key Points

**1. God Has Appointed a Day of Judgment**
God has appointed a day in which He will judge the world in righteousness through Jesus Christ. The Father has given all power and judgment to the Son (citing Acts 17:31; John 5:22).

**2. Who Will Be Judged**
All persons who have ever lived will appear before the judgment seat of Christ to give account of their thoughts, words, and deeds. This includes:
- All people from history
- Apostate angels (fallen angels)

**3. Purpose of the Judgment**
The judgment is for:
- The manifestation of God's glory—His mercy in the salvation of the elect and His justice in the damnation of the reprobate
- The righteous receiving everlasting life and "fullness of joy and refreshing" in the presence of the Lord
- The wicked being cast into eternal torments and punished with everlasting destruction

**4. The Practical Purpose of This Doctrine**
The Confession states that Christ would have us:
- Be **certainly persuaded** that there will be a day of judgment, to deter all from sin
- Find **greater consolation** for the godly in their adversity
- Be **watchful**, since the day is unknown, ready to say, "Come, Lord Jesus; come quickly. Amen"

**5. The Day Is Unknown**
Just as Christ would have us shake off carnal security, He has kept the day unknown so we will always be prepared—not knowing the hour when the Lord will come.

## Related Sections

The Confession also addresses related themes in:
- **Chapter 32** ("Of the State of Men after Death, and of the Resurrection of the Dead") — bodily resurrection of both the just and unjust
- **Chapter 8** — Christ's role as Mediator and Judge

The doctrine reflects historic Reformed eschatology, emphasizing both God's justice and mercy while urging believers toward holiness, perseverance, and hopeful expectation of Christ's return.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561), one of the foundational doctrinal standards of the Reformed churches, addresses the doctrine of God primarily in its opening articles. Here's what it teaches about the only God:

## Article 1: There Is One Only God

The Confession states that "we all believe with the heart and confess with the mouth that there is one only simple and spiritual Being, which we call God."

It then ascribes to God several essential attributes:
- **Eternal** – without beginning or end
- **Incomprehensible** – beyond full human understanding
- **Invisible** – cannot be seen with physical eyes
- **Immutable** – unchanging
- **Infinite** – without limits
- **Almighty** – all-powerful
- **Perfectly wise** – possessing complete wisdom
- **Just** – perfectly righteous
- **Good** – the source of all goodness
- **The overflowing fountain of all good**

## Article 2: The Means by Which We Know God

The Confession teaches that God is known by two means:
1. **Creation** – the universe is "before our eyes as a most elegant book, wherein all creatures, great and small, are as so many characters leading us to contemplate the invisible things of God"
2. **Scripture** – God makes Himself "more clearly and fully known to us by His holy and divine Word"

## Articles 8–9: The Trinity

While affirming one God, the Confession teaches that this one divine essence subsists in three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. These three are distinct in their personal properties but share one undivided essence, eternally co-equal and co-eternal.

## Key Emphasis

The Confession draws heavily from passages like Deuteronomy 6:4 ("Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one") and presents God as both transcendent (beyond creation) and the source of all good gifts. The doctrine reflects classical Christian theism shaped by Reformed convictions about God's sovereignty and self-revelation.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561), one of the foundational Reformed confessional documents written primarily by Guido de Brès, addresses how we know God in its first two articles. It teaches that God is known through **two means**, often called the "two books" of revelation:

## Article 2: The Two Means of Knowing God

**1. General Revelation — The "Book of Nature"**

We know God "by the creation, preservation, and government of the universe, which is before our eyes as a most beautiful book, wherein all creatures, great and small, are as so many letters leading us to perceive clearly the invisible things of God, namely, His eternal power and divinity, as the apostle Paul says in Romans 1:20."

Through creation itself, all people can perceive something of God's existence and attributes—particularly His power and divine nature.

**2. Special Revelation — The "Holy and Divine Word"**

God makes Himself known "more clearly and fully" by "His holy and divine Word; that is to say, as far as is necessary for us to know in this life, to His glory and our salvation."

Scripture provides the clearer, fuller, and saving knowledge of God that creation alone cannot give.

## Key Theological Points

- **Sufficiency of Scripture**: Articles 3–7 elaborate that the Bible is divinely inspired, canonical, sufficient, and authoritative—superior to all human writings, traditions, or church decrees.

- **Priority of Special Revelation**: While creation reveals God truly, it is insufficient for salvation. Scripture is necessary to know God savingly.

- **Self-Authentication**: The Confession teaches (Article 5) that we receive these Scriptures as holy and canonical not primarily because the Church says so, but "because the Holy Ghost witnesseth in our hearts that they are from God."

- **Limits of Knowledge**: We know God "as far as is necessary for us to know in this life"—the Confession acknowledges that our knowledge is real but not exhaustive.

This twofold framework (nature and Scripture) became standard in Reformed theology and is echoed in later documents like the Westminster Confession of Faith (1.1).

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561), written primarily by Guido de Brès, addresses the sufficiency of Scripture mainly in **Articles 5-7**. Here's a summary of its teaching:

## Article 3: The Written Word of God
Establishes that Scripture comes from God, with holy men writing as they were "moved by the Holy Spirit" (citing 2 Peter 1:21).

## Article 5: The Authority of Scripture
Affirms that we receive the canonical books "for the regulation, foundation, and confirmation of our faith." Their authority comes not from the Church but from the Holy Spirit's witness in believers' hearts, and from the books carrying "the evidence thereof in themselves."

## Article 7: The Sufficiency of Holy Scripture
This is the most explicit statement on sufficiency. Key teachings include:

1. **Scripture fully contains God's will**: "We believe that those Holy Scriptures fully contain the will of God, and that whatsoever man ought to believe unto salvation is sufficiently taught therein."

2. **Nothing may be added or taken away**: "It is unlawful for any one, though an apostle, to teach otherwise than we are now taught in the Holy Scriptures."

3. **Scripture is the supreme standard**: No writings of men, customs, traditions, councils, decrees, or statutes can be set on equal footing with Scripture. "The truth is above all."

4. **Tests for all teaching**: All things must be "examined, regulated, and reformed according to" Scripture.

5. **Rejects supplementary authorities**: Specifically rejects placing church tradition, councils, or human writings on par with the Bible.

## Significance

This article reflects the Reformation principle of **sola Scriptura** in distinction from the Roman Catholic position (formalized at Trent, 1546) that placed unwritten tradition alongside Scripture as a source of authority. It also guards against subjective revelations or claimed prophecies that would add to the biblical canon.

The Belgic Confession remains a doctrinal standard in Reformed churches, particularly those of Dutch and Belgian heritage (the "Three Forms of Unity" along with the Heidelberg Catechism and Canons of Dort).

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561), one of the foundational doctrinal standards of the Reformed churches, addresses the creation of all things primarily in **Article 12, "The Creation of All Things."**

Here is a summary of what it teaches:

## Key Teachings on Creation

**1. God is the Creator of all things**
The Confession states that the Father, "when it seemed good to him, created heaven and earth and all other creatures from nothing, by the Word—that is to say, by his Son." This affirms *creatio ex nihilo* (creation out of nothing).

**2. God gave every creature its being, shape, and form**
He gave each creature "its being, shape, form, and several offices to serve its Creator." Creation is purposeful and ordered, not random.

**3. Creation continues to be sustained by God**
God continues to "sustain and govern them all, according to his eternal providence and by his infinite power, that they may serve man, in order that man may serve God."

**4. The creation of angels**
The Confession specifically addresses the creation of angels:
- God created them good, to be his messengers and to serve his elect
- Some angels fell from their original excellency into eternal perdition (the devils and evil spirits)
- The remaining angels persisted in their original state by the grace of God
- The devils and evil spirits are corrupt and lie in wait to ruin the Church and every member of it

**5. Rejection of error**
The article rejects the error of the Sadducees, who denied the existence of spirits and angels, and the error of the Manichees, who taught that devils have their origin of themselves and are evil by their own nature rather than by their depravation.

## Related Articles

- **Article 2** teaches that God is known by two means: the creation, preservation, and government of the universe (which is "before our eyes as a most elegant book"), and more clearly by his holy and divine Word.
- **Article 13** addresses God's providence in governing his creation.
- **Article 14** discusses the creation and fall of humanity specifically.

The Confession's teaching on creation emphasizes God's sovereignty, the goodness of creation, the purposeful design of all things, and creation's role in serving God's glory.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the doctrine of god's providence?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that this good God, after creating all things, did not abandon them to chance or fortune but leads and governs them according to his holy will, in such a way that nothing happens in this world without God's orderly arrangement. Yet God is not the author of, and cannot be charged with, the sin that occurs. For God's power and goodness are so great and incomprehensible that God arranges and does his works very well and justly even when the devils and the wicked act unjustly. We do not wish to inquire with undue curiosity into what God does that surpasses human understanding and is beyond our ability to comprehend. But in all humility and reverence we adore the just judgments of God, which are hidden from us, being content to be Christ's disciples, so as to learn only what God shows us in the Word, without going beyond those limits. This doctrine gives us unspeakable comfort since it teaches us that nothing can happen to us by chance but only by the arrangement of our gracious heavenly Father, who watches over us with fatherly care, sustaining all creatures under his lordship, so that not one of the hairs on our heads (for they are all numbered) nor even a little bird can fall to the ground without the will of our Father. (Matt. 10:29-30) In this thought we rest, knowing that God holds in check the devils and all our enemies, who cannot hurt us without divine permission and will. For that reason we reject the damnable error of the Epicureans, who say that God does not get involved in anything and leaves everything to chance.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561), one of the doctrinal standards of Reformed churches (part of the "Three Forms of Unity"), addresses God's providence primarily in **Article 13**, titled "The Doctrine of God's Providence."

## Key Teachings

**1. God's Sovereign Governance of All Things**
The Confession teaches that after God created all things, He did not abandon them to chance or fortune but "leads and governs them according to his holy will, in such a way that nothing happens in this world without his orderly arrangement."

**2. God Is Not the Author of Sin**
While affirming God's complete sovereignty, the Confession carefully states that God is not the author of sin, nor can He be charged with the sins committed. His power and goodness are "so great and incomprehensible" that He orders and executes His work in the most excellent and just manner even when devils and wicked men act unjustly.

**3. The Mystery of Providence**
The Confession acknowledges that God's works surpass human understanding. It warns against curiously inquiring into things beyond what God has revealed, instead urging believers to humbly adore the just judgments of God which are hidden from us.

**4. Comfort for Believers**
This doctrine provides "unspeakable consolation" because it teaches us that:
- Nothing happens by chance
- All things come by the direction of our gracious heavenly Father
- God watches over us with fatherly care
- Not a hair can fall from our heads, nor a sparrow to the ground, without the will of our Father (citing Matthew 10:29-30)

**5. Rejection of Epicurean Error**
The Confession rejects "the damnable error of the Epicureans, who say that God regards nothing but leaves all things to chance."

## Significance

This article reflects classical Reformed teaching, balancing God's absolute sovereignty over all events with human responsibility for sin, while emphasizing the pastoral comfort this doctrine offers to believers who trust in their heavenly Father's loving care.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the creation and fall of humanity?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that God created human beings from the dust of the earth and made and formed them in his image and likeness- good, just, and holy; able by their will to conform in all things to the will of God. But when they were in honor they did not understand it (Ps. 49:20) and did not recognize their excellence. But they subjected themselves willingly to sin and consequently to death and the curse, lending their ear to the word of the devil. For they transgressed the commandment of life, which they had received, and by their sin they separated themselves from God, who was their true life, having corrupted their entire nature. So they made themselves guilty and subject to physical and spiritual death, having become wicked, perverse, and corrupt in all their ways. They lost all their excellent gifts which they had received from God, and retained none of them except for small traces which are enough to make them inexcusable. Moreover, all the light in us is turned to darkness, as the Scripture teaches us: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it." (John 1:5) Here John calls the human race "darkness." Therefore we reject everything taught to the contrary concerning human free will, since humans are nothing but the slaves of sin and cannot do a thing unless it is given them from heaven. (John 3:27) For who can boast of being able to do anything good by oneself, since Christ says, "No one can come to me unless drawn by the Father who sent me"? (John 6:44) Who can glory in their own will when they understand that "the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God"? (Rom. 8:7) Who can speak of their own knowledge in view of the fact that "those who are unspiritual do not receive the gifts of God's Spirit"? (1 Cor. 2:14) In short, who can produce a single thought, knowing that we are not able to think a thing about ourselves, by ourselves, but that "our competence is from God"? (2 Cor. 3:5) And therefore, what the apostle says ought rightly to stand fixed and firm: God works within us both to will and to do according to his good pleasure. (Phil. 2:13) For there is no understanding nor will conforming to God's understanding and will apart from Christ's involvement, as he teaches us when he says, "Apart from me you can do nothing." (John 15:5)

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561), written primarily by Guido de Brès, addresses the creation and fall of humanity mainly in **Articles 14 and 15**. Here's a summary of its teaching:

## Article 14: The Creation and Fall of Humanity

**On Creation:**
- God created humanity "from the dust of the earth" and made man in His own image and likeness—"good, righteous, and holy."
- Humanity was created with a will that could conform to God's will in every respect.
- Adam was given the ability to live in harmony with God's purposes.

**On the Fall:**
- When Adam was in honor, he did not appreciate it or recognize his excellence.
- He willfully subjected himself to sin and consequently to death and the curse by listening to the devil.
- By transgressing God's commandment of life, Adam separated himself from God, who was his true life.
- Adam corrupted his entire nature, making himself liable to physical and spiritual death.

**Consequences of the Fall:**
- Humanity became wicked, perverse, and corrupt in all its ways.
- Humans lost all their excellent gifts received from God, retaining only small traces (sufficient to render them inexcusable).
- All the light in us has turned to darkness, as Scripture teaches (citing John 1:5).
- Free will is rejected as a Pelagian error—humans are "slaves of sin" and can receive nothing unless it is given from heaven (John 3:27).

## Article 15: The Doctrine of Original Sin

- Original sin is described as a **hereditary corruption** that extends to the whole human race.
- It is a corruption of the entire human nature—an inherited depravity that even infects infants in their mother's womb.
- This sin produces in humanity every sort of sin, acting as a "root" from which sins spring.
- Original sin is so vile and enormous that it is sufficient to condemn the human race.
- It is **not abolished or eradicated even by baptism**, though Christ's grace through forgiveness does not impute it to believers for condemnation.
- The confession rejects the Pelagian view that this sin is merely imitation.

## Theological Significance

The Belgic Confession reflects classic **Reformed/Calvinist anthropology**:
1. **Total depravity** – sin affects every aspect of human nature
2. **Original sin as inherited guilt and corruption** – not merely a bad example
3. **Rejection of Pelagianism and semi-Pelagianism** – humans cannot save themselves
4. **Humans remain responsible** – traces of God's image leave us "without excuse"
5. **Grace alone** – sets up the necessity of Christ's redemptive work, developed in subsequent articles

This teaching laid groundwork for the confession's later articles on Christ's atonement and salvation by grace alone, making it foundational to Reformed soteriology in the Dutch and broader Continental Reformed tradition.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the doctrine of original sin?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that by the disobedience of Adam original sin has been spread through the whole human race. (Rom. 5:12-13) It is a corruption of the whole human nature- an inherited depravity which even infects small infants in their mother's womb, and the root which produces in humanity every sort of sin. It is therefore so vile and enormous in God's sight that it is enough to condemn the human race, and it is not abolished or wholly uprooted even by baptism, seeing that sin constantly boils forth as though from a contaminated spring. Nevertheless, it is not imputed to God's children for their condemnation but is forgiven by his grace and mercy- not to put them to sleep but so that the awareness of this corruption might often make believers groan as they long to be set free from the body of this death. (Rom. 7:24) Therefore we reject the error of the Pelagians who say that this sin is nothing else than a matter of imitation.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561), one of the doctrinal standards of the Reformed churches (along with the Heidelberg Catechism and Canons of Dort, forming the "Three Forms of Unity"), addresses original sin primarily in **Article 15**, titled "The Doctrine of Original Sin."

## Key Teachings of Article 15

**1. Origin and Transmission**
The Confession teaches that original sin is "a corruption of the whole human nature" which is an inherited depravity "extending to all mankind." It is propagated from Adam to his entire posterity—not merely by imitation, but by "the propagation of a vicious nature."

**2. Nature of the Corruption**
Original sin is described as so deep and pervasive that:
- It is "sufficient to condemn all mankind"
- Not even infants in their mother's womb are excluded—they too are guilty
- It produces in human nature "all sorts of sin," being "the root" from which actual sins spring

**3. Persistence in the Regenerate**
Importantly, the Confession states that original sin is **not entirely abolished even by baptism**. It remains in believers throughout their lives, though God in His grace does not impute it to His children for condemnation. Believers must continually groan under this corruption and long for deliverance.

**4. Rejection of Pelagianism**
The article explicitly rejects "the error of the Pelagians, who assert that sin proceeds only from imitation." This affirms the Augustinian and Reformed view that sin is a hereditary condition, not merely learned behavior.

## Related Articles

- **Article 14** ("The Creation and Fall of Man") provides the backdrop, teaching that Adam, through willful disobedience, "subjected himself to spiritual and temporal death" and corrupted his whole nature, becoming wicked, perverse, and corrupt in all his ways.
- **Article 16** then moves to election, showing that God's mercy rescues some from this common ruin.

## Theological Significance

The Belgic Confession's treatment is thoroughly Augustinian and aligns with Calvin's teaching on total depravity. It maintains:
- The **universality** of original sin
- The **hereditary** nature of corruption
- The **gravity** sufficient for condemnation
- The **persistence** of indwelling sin even in the redeemed
- The **necessity** of divine grace for salvation

Author Guido de Brès wrote the Confession largely to demonstrate that Reformed believers held orthodox Christian doctrine, and the article on original sin reflects mainstream Western catholic teaching while sharpening it against Pelagian and Anabaptist tendencies of the time.

God is merciful in withdrawing and saving from this perdition those who, in the eternal and unchangeable divine counsel, have been elected and chosen in Jesus Christ our Lord by his pure goodness, without any consideration of their works. questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561), one of the Three Forms of Unity in Reformed churches, addresses the doctrine of election primarily in **Article 16, "The Doctrine of Election."**

## Key Teachings

**1. The Fall and Universal Corruption**
The article begins by affirming that the entire human race fell into perdition and ruin through the sin of the first parents. All humanity, by nature, is deserving of condemnation.

**2. God's Mercy and Justice**
The confession teaches that God revealed Himself to be both **merciful and just** in response to humanity's fallen state:
- **Merciful**: in delivering and preserving from perdition those whom He has elected in Christ Jesus, by His pure goodness, without any consideration of their works.
- **Just**: in leaving others in their fall and perdition, in which they have involved themselves.

**3. Election in Christ**
Election is specifically **"in Christ Jesus our Lord"**—it is not abstract but Christocentric. The elect are chosen in Christ from before the foundation of the world.

**4. Unconditional Election**
The confession explicitly states that election is based on God's **"pure goodness"** and not on any foreseen works or merit in the elect. This affirms the Reformed doctrine of unconditional election.

**5. Eternal and Unchangeable**
God's decree of election is described as eternal and unchangeable, rooted in His sovereign will before creation.

## Theological Context

This article reflects classic Reformed (Calvinistic) soteriology and predates the more detailed treatment found in the **Canons of Dort** (1618-1619), which were written to defend these same principles against Arminian objections. The Belgic Confession presents election with pastoral restraint—emphasizing God's mercy and goodness toward the elect while affirming His justice in the reprobation of others without dwelling extensively on the latter.

The doctrine is presented not as speculative theology but as a comfort: salvation depends entirely on God's sovereign grace, not human merit.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the righteousness of faith?
questions.reference_answer: We believe that for us to acquire the true knowledge of this great mystery the Holy Spirit kindles in our hearts a true faith that embraces Jesus Christ, with all his merits, and makes him its own, and no longer looks for anything apart from him. For it must necessarily follow that either all that is required for our salvation is not in Christ or, if all is in him, then those who have Christ by faith have his salvation entirely. Therefore, to say that Christ is not enough but that something else is needed as well is a most enormous blasphemy against God- for it then would follow that Jesus Christ is only half a Savior. And therefore we justly say with Paul that we are justified "by faith alone" or "by faith apart from works." (Rom. 3:28) However, we do not mean, properly speaking, that it is faith itself that justifies us- for faith is only the instrument by which we embrace Christ, our righteousness. But Jesus Christ is our righteousness in making available to us all his merits and all the holy works he has done for us and in our place. And faith is the instrument that keeps us in communion with him and with all his benefits. When those benefits are made ours, they are more than enough to absolve us of our sins.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561), one of the foundational doctrinal standards of Reformed churches, addresses the righteousness of faith primarily in **Article 22** ("The Righteousness of Faith") and **Article 23** ("The Justification of Sinners"). Here is what it teaches:

## Article 22: The Righteousness of Faith

1. **Faith is the instrument that embraces Christ.** The Holy Spirit kindles true faith in our hearts, and this faith embraces Jesus Christ with all His merits, making Him our own and seeking nothing besides Him.

2. **Christ's merits are imputed, not faith itself.** The Confession is careful to clarify that faith is not the *ground* of our righteousness, but the *means* by which we receive it. It states: "We do not mean that faith itself justifies us, for it is only an instrument with which we embrace Christ, our righteousness."

3. **Christ Himself is our righteousness.** Jesus Christ, "imputing to us all His merits and so many holy works which He has done for us and in our stead, is our righteousness."

4. **Faith keeps us in communion with Christ.** Faith holds us in fellowship with Christ in all His benefits, which become ours and are more than sufficient to acquit us of our sins.

## Article 23: The Justification of Sinners

1. **Our blessedness lies in forgiveness through Christ.** Our righteousness before God consists in the forgiveness of our sins, in which our blessedness is found (citing Psalm 32 and Romans 4).

2. **Rejection of merit.** We cannot rely on any works, neither our own nor any merit of our own, but rest solely on the obedience of Christ crucified, which is ours when we believe in Him.

3. **Sufficient to cover all sin.** Christ's righteousness is sufficient to cover all our iniquities and gives us confidence in approaching God, freeing our consciences from fear and dread.

4. **Humility and dependence.** This doctrine keeps us humble, prevents us from being presumptuous, and makes us cling to Christ alone—since apart from Him we would always be doubtful and tossed about.

## Key Theological Points

- **Sola Fide (Faith Alone):** Justification is by faith alone, but faith itself is not meritorious.
- **Imputed Righteousness:** Christ's perfect obedience and satisfaction are credited to the believer.
- **Christ-centered:** The focus is consistently on Christ as the object and substance of our righteousness, not on the quality or strength of our faith.
- **Assurance and Humility:** This doctrine produces both confidence before God and humility in ourselves.

The Belgic Confession thus stands firmly in the Reformation tradition, echoing the teaching of Paul (especially Romans 3–5) and aligning with other Reformed standards like the Heidelberg Catechism (Q&A 60–61) on justification by faith alone in Christ alone.

questions.question: What does the Belgic Confession teach about the last judgement?
questions.reference_answer: Finally we believe, according to God's Word, that when the time appointed by the Lord is come (which is unknown to all creatures) and the number of the elect is complete, our Lord Jesus Christ will come from heaven, bodily and visibly, as he ascended, with great glory and majesty, to declare himself the judge of the living and the dead. He will burn this old world, in fire and flame, in order to cleanse it. Then all human creatures will appear in person before the great judge- men, women, and children, who have lived from the beginning until the end of the world. They will be summoned there "with the archangel's call and with the sound of God's trumpet." (1 Thess. 4:16) For all those who died before that time will be raised from the earth, their spirits being joined and united with their own bodies in which they lived. And as for those who are still alive, they will not die like the others but will be changed "in the twinkling of an eye" from perishable to imperishable. (1 Cor. 15:51-53) Then the books (that is, the consciences) will be opened, and the dead will be judged according to the things they did in the world, (Rev. 20:12) whether good or evil. Indeed, all people will give account of all the idle words they have spoken, (Matt. 12:36) which the world regards as only playing games. And then the secrets and hypocrisies of all people will be publicly uncovered in the sight of all. Therefore, with good reason the thought of this judgment is horrible and dreadful to wicked and evil people. But it is very pleasant and a great comfort to the righteous and elect, since their total redemption will then be accomplished. They will then receive the fruits of their labor and of the trouble they have suffered; their innocence will be openly recognized by all; and they will see the terrible vengeance that God will bring on the evil ones who tyrannized, oppressed, and tormented them in this world. The evil ones will be convicted by the witness of their own consciences, and shall be made immortal- but only to be tormented in "the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels." (Matt. 25:41) In contrast, the faithful and elect will be crowned with glory and honor. The Son of God will profess their names (Matt. 10:32) before God his Father and the holy and elect angels; all tears will be wiped from their eyes; (Rev. 7:17) and their cause- at present condemned as heretical and evil by many judges and civil officers- will be acknowledged as the cause of the Son of God. And as a gracious reward the Lord will make them possess a glory such as the human heart could never imagine. So we look forward to that great day with longing in order to enjoy fully the promises of God in Christ Jesus, our Lord.

questions.response:
The Belgic Confession (1561), one of the Three Forms of Unity in Reformed churches, addresses the Last Judgment primarily in **Article 37**, its final and longest article. Here are its main teachings:

## Key Points

**1. Christ's Return**
Christ will return bodily and visibly from heaven "with great glory and majesty" at the time appointed by God (which is unknown to all creatures). His coming will declare himself Judge of the living and the dead.

**2. Resurrection of All People**
All the dead will be raised from the earth, their souls reunited with their own bodies. Those still living at Christ's return will not die but will be "changed from corruptible to incorruptible."

**3. Opening of the Books**
The "books" (the conscience) will be opened, and the dead judged according to what they did in this world, whether good or evil. All people will give account of every idle word spoken.

**4. Separation of the Righteous and Wicked**
- The **wicked** (including devils) will be condemned to eternal torment in "everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels."
- The **faithful and elect** will be crowned with glory and honor, publicly acknowledged by Christ, and vindicated before all.

**5. Comfort for Believers**
The article uniquely emphasizes that the thought of judgment is **"a great consolation"** to the godly and elect, because:
- Their full deliverance will be accomplished
- They will receive the fruits of their labor
- Their innocence will be made known to all
- They will see the terrible vengeance God brings on the wicked who persecuted them
- Their cause (currently condemned by many judges as heretical) will be vindicated

**6. The Reward of Believers**
The faithful will receive glory "such as the heart of man could never conceive." They will enter into eternal joy with Christ.

## Distinctive Emphasis

What's notable about the Belgic Confession's treatment is its **pastoral tone**—written during a time of persecution (its author, Guido de Brès, was later martyred), it presents the Last Judgment not primarily as terror but as the believer's ultimate vindication and comfort, when wrongs will be righted and Christ will publicly own his people.

questions.reference_answer:
Election is the unchangeable purpose of God, whereby, before the foundation of the world, He hath out of mere grace, according to the sovereign good pleasure of His own will, chosen, from the whole human race, which had fallen through their own fault from their primitive state of rectitude into sin and destruction, a certain number of persons to redemption in Christ, whom He from eternity appointed the Mediator and Head of the elect, and the foundation of salvation.

This elect number, though by nature neither better nor more deserving than others, but with them involved in one common misery, God hath decreed to give to Christ, to be saved by Him, and effectually to call and draw them to His communion by His Word and Spirit, to bestow upon them true faith, justification and sanctification; and having powerfully preserved them in the fellowship of His Son, finally, to glorify them for the demonstration of His mercy and for the praise of His glorious grace, as it is written: "According as He hath chosen us in Him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before Him in love: having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to Himself, according to the good pleasure of His will, to the praise of the glory of His grace, wherein He hath made us accepted in the beloved" (Eph. 1:4-6). And elsewhere: "Whom He did predestinate, them He also called: and whom He called, them He also justified: and whom He justified them He also glorified" (Rom. 8:30).

questions.response:
The Canons of Dort, in the First Head of Doctrine, Article 7, provide a classic Reformed definition of election. Here is a summary of what is taught:

**Definition of Election**

Article 7 defines election as the unchangeable purpose of God by which, before the foundation of the world, He has out of mere grace, according to the sovereign good pleasure of His own will, chosen from the whole human race (which had fallen by its own fault from its original integrity into sin and ruin) a certain number of persons to redemption in Christ.

**Key Elements Taught**

1. **Eternal** – Election took place before the foundation of the world, not in time.

2. **Unchangeable** – God's purpose cannot be altered or frustrated.

3. **Gracious** – It proceeds from mere grace, not from any merit or foreseen worthiness in the elect.

4. **Sovereign** – It flows from the good pleasure of God's will alone.

5. **Particular** – A definite number of specific persons are chosen, not a vague or indefinite group.

6. **From a fallen mass** – The elect are chosen out of humanity considered as already fallen in sin (this reflects the "infralapsarian" framing the Synod adopted).

7. **In Christ** – Christ is appointed as the Mediator, Head, and foundation of salvation for the elect.

8. **Unto salvation** – The elect are chosen not only to salvation itself but also to the means of salvation: faith, justification, sanctification, and glorification.

The article concludes by affirming that God decreed to give the elect to Christ, to effectually call and draw them into His communion by His Word and Spirit, to bestow true faith, justify and sanctify them, and finally glorify them—all to the praise of His glorious grace.

This article is foundational to the Reformed doctrine of unconditional election, one of the so-called "five points of Calvinism" that emerged in response to the Arminian Remonstrance.

questions.response:
The Canons of Dort, in the First Head of Doctrine, Article 9, teach that election is **not based on foreseen faith, obedience, or any other quality or disposition in the person**. Rather, election is the **source** (or cause) of faith and holiness, not their result.

The article states that God chose people to faith and to the obedience of faith, to holiness, etc. Therefore, election is the fountain of every saving good, from which flow faith, holiness, and the other gifts of salvation, including eternal life itself, as its fruits and effects. As the Apostle Paul says: "He chose us [not because we were, but] that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:4).

Key points of Article 9:

1. **Election is unconditional** — it does not depend on anything foreseen in the person being elected (such as their future faith or good works).

2. **Election is the cause of faith**, not its consequence. Faith and holiness are the *fruits* of election, not the *grounds* for it.

3. **It cites Ephesians 1:4** as scriptural support, emphasizing that God chose believers *so that* they would be holy — meaning holiness is the purpose and result of election, not its condition.

questions.response:
# Canons of Dort, Second Head of Doctrine, Article 1

The Second Head of Doctrine in the Canons of Dort addresses "The Death of Christ and the Redemption of Men Thereby." Article 1 states:

**"God is not only supremely merciful, but also supremely just. And his justice requires (as he hath revealed himself in his Word) that our sins committed against his infinite majesty should be punished, not only with temporal but with eternal punishments, both in body and soul; which we cannot escape, unless satisfaction be made to the justice of God."**

## Key Teachings of Article 1:

1. **God's dual attributes**: God is both supremely merciful *and* supremely just. These attributes are held together, not in tension where one cancels the other.

2. **The demand of divine justice**: God's justice requires that sin be punished. This is not arbitrary but flows from who God is.

3. **The gravity of sin**: Sin is committed against God's "infinite majesty," which is why it deserves infinite (eternal) punishment.

4. **The nature of the punishment**: The penalty for sin includes:
   - Both **temporal** and **eternal** punishment
   - Both **body** and **soul**

5. **The necessity of satisfaction**: There is no escape from this punishment *unless* satisfaction is made to God's justice. This sets up the rest of the section, which explains how Christ's death provides that satisfaction.

## Significance

Article 1 lays the foundation for understanding the atonement by establishing *why* Christ's death was necessary. Before discussing the nature and extent of Christ's redemptive work (a key issue against the Arminian Remonstrants), the Synod first grounds everything in God's just character and the seriousness of human sin. The cross is not merely an expression of love but a legal and moral necessity given God's righteous nature.

# Canons of Dort, Second Head of Doctrine, Article 8

Article 8 of the Second Head of Doctrine (which addresses "The Death of Christ and the Redemption of Men Thereby") teaches the doctrine commonly known as **particular redemption** or **definite atonement**.

## The Teaching of Article 8

The article states that it was the sovereign counsel, gracious will, and purpose of God the Father that the **quickening and saving efficacy** of Christ's most precious death should extend to **all the elect**, for the purpose of:

1. **Bestowing upon them alone the gift of justifying faith**, thereby infallibly bringing them to salvation
2. **Effectually redeeming** from every people, tribe, nation, and language all those—and only those—who were from eternity **chosen to salvation** and given to Christ by the Father
3. **Conferring upon them faith**, which (together with all other saving gifts of the Holy Spirit) Christ purchased for them by His death
4. **Cleansing them by His blood** from all sins, both original and actual, whether committed before or after believing
5. **Preserving them faithfully** to the end
6. **Presenting them finally without spot or blemish** before His presence in glory

## Key Points

- The death of Christ was **purposeful and effectual**, not merely potential. It actually accomplishes salvation for those for whom it was intended.
- The atonement is **particular in its design**—directed by God's eternal decree toward the elect specifically.
- Christ's death **purchased not only the possibility of salvation but also faith itself** and all the gifts necessary to bring the elect to glory.
- The scope is **universal in extent across humanity** ("every people, tribe, nation, and language") while particular as to individuals (the elect).

This article was crafted in response to the Remonstrant (Arminian) view that Christ died for all people equally, making salvation merely possible but contingent on human response. The Synod of Dort (1618–1619) affirmed instead that Christ's atonement actually secures the salvation of all those for whom He died.

The Canons of Dort address the corruption of man and his conversion to God in the **Third and Fourth Heads of Doctrine** (these two heads are combined in the Canons).

**Article 1 of the Third and Fourth Heads of Doctrine** teaches the following about man's corruption:

Man was originally created in the image of God. He was endowed with:
- **True and saving knowledge** of his Creator and spiritual things
- **Righteousness** in his will and heart
- **Holiness** (purity) in all his affections
- And was thus **wholly holy**

However, through the instigation of the devil and by his own free will, man **revolted from God** and **deprived himself of these excellent gifts**. In their place, he brought upon himself:
- **Blindness of mind**
- **Horrible darkness**
- **Vanity and perverseness of judgment**
- **Wickedness, rebellion, and hardness** in his heart and will
- **Impurity** in all his affections

The article emphasizes that this fall was the result of man's own willful disobedience, not God's doing, and that the consequences were comprehensive—affecting the mind, will, heart, and affections of man.

This article sets the foundation for the Reformed doctrine of **total depravity**, showing that the entire human nature was corrupted by the fall, which is why man cannot save himself and must be regenerated by God's sovereign grace (as developed in the subsequent articles).

questions.response:
The **Canons of Dort**, Third and Fourth Heads of Doctrine (which are typically treated together), Article 3, teaches the following about the corruption of man:

**Article 3 (Third/Fourth Head of Doctrine):**

"Therefore all men are conceived in sin, and are by nature children of wrath, incapable of saving good, prone to evil, dead in sin, and in bondage thereto, and without the regenerating grace of the Holy Spirit, they are neither able nor willing to return to God, to reform the depravity of their nature, nor to dispose themselves to reformation."

**Key teachings of this article:**

1. **Universal sinfulness** – All people are conceived in sin (referencing Psalm 51:5).

2. **Children of wrath by nature** – Drawing from Ephesians 2:3, humanity stands under God's judgment from birth.

3. **Total inability** – Man is "incapable of saving good," meaning he cannot perform anything that contributes to his salvation.

4. **Inclination toward evil** – Human nature is "prone to evil."

5. **Spiritual death and bondage** – Man is "dead in sin, and in bondage thereto" (echoing Ephesians 2:1 and John 8:34).

6. **Necessity of regenerating grace** – Without the Holy Spirit's regenerating work, fallen man is:
   - Unable to return to God
   - Unwilling to return to God
   - Unable to reform his own depravity
   - Unable to even dispose himself toward reformation

This article forms part of the Reformed doctrine of **total depravity**, emphasizing that conversion to God is entirely a work of God's sovereign grace, since fallen humanity has neither the ability nor the desire to turn to God on its own. It was written in response to the Arminian (Remonstrant) view that humans retain some natural ability to cooperate with or initiate their conversion.

questions.response:
The Canons of Dort, in the Third and Fourth Heads of Doctrine, Article 10, address the conversion of man and attribute it entirely to God's grace rather than to human merit or free will.

**Summary of Article 10 (Third and Fourth Heads of Doctrine):**

The article teaches that the fact that some people, when called through the gospel, come and are converted is **not to be attributed to man**, as though one distinguishes himself by his free will from others who are equally furnished with grace sufficient for faith and conversion (as the Pelagian heresy maintains). 

Rather, conversion **must be wholly ascribed to God**, who:
- From eternity has chosen His own in Christ
- Effectually calls them in time
- Confers upon them faith and repentance
- Rescues them from the power of darkness
- Translates them into the kingdom of His own Son

This is done so that they may show forth the praises of Him who called them out of darkness into His marvelous light, and may glory not in themselves but in the Lord, as the apostolic writings frequently testify.

**Key Theological Points:**

1. **Rejection of Pelagianism/Semi-Pelagianism** – The article explicitly denies that the difference between those who believe and those who don't lies in man's own will or cooperation.

2. **Monergism** – Conversion is the work of God alone, not a synergistic effort between God and man.

3. **Doxological Purpose** – The end of conversion is that God receives all glory, and the believer boasts only in the Lord.

4. **Scriptural Grounding** – The article appeals to passages like 1 Peter 2:9 and 1 Corinthians 1:31 ("He that glories, let him glory in the Lord").

This article stands as a clear affirmation of the Reformed doctrine of irresistible (or efficacious) grace, the "I" in the TULIP acronym.

# Canons of Dort, Third and Fourth Heads of Doctrine, Article 11

Article 11 addresses **"The Holy Spirit's Work in Conversion"** and teaches the following:

When God carries out His good pleasure in the elect, or works true conversion in them, He not only causes the gospel to be outwardly preached to them and powerfully illuminates their minds by the Holy Spirit so that they may rightly understand and discern the things of the Spirit of God. But by the efficacy of the same regenerating Spirit, He also:

1. **Penetrates into the inmost being of man**
2. **Opens the closed heart**
3. **Softens the hard heart**
4. **Circumcises the heart that is uncircumcised**
5. **Infuses new qualities into the will**, making the will which was dead, alive; which was bad, good; which was unwilling, willing; and which was stubborn, compliant
6. **Actuates and strengthens the will** so that, like a good tree, it may be able to produce the fruits of good actions

The article emphasizes that conversion is not merely an external matter of moral persuasion or the offering of the gospel outwardly, but involves a deep, internal, supernatural work of the Holy Spirit who actually transforms the faculties of the soul—particularly the mind and the will.

This article guards against:
- **Pelagianism and semi-Pelagianism**, which would make conversion depend on human cooperation or natural ability
- **Mere moral suasion theories**, which reduce regeneration to external influence rather than internal renewal

The teaching reflects the Reformed conviction that regeneration is **monergistic**—God alone is the efficient cause of the new birth, working powerfully within the sinner to bring about genuine spiritual change.

questions.response:
The Canons of Dort, in the Fifth Head of Doctrine, Article 1, teach the following about the perseverance of the saints:

**"Those whom God, according to His purpose, calls to the communion of His Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and regenerates by the Holy Spirit, He also delivers from the dominion and slavery of sin, though in this life He does not deliver them altogether from the body of sin and from the infirmities of the flesh."**

Key teachings of this article:

1. **Divine initiative**: God calls believers according to His purpose into fellowship with Christ.

2. **Regeneration by the Spirit**: Those called are regenerated (born again) by the Holy Spirit.

3. **Deliverance from sin's dominion**: The regenerate are freed from the *reigning power* and *slavery* of sin — sin no longer rules them as master.

4. **Continuing struggle**: However, in this present life, believers are *not* completely delivered from:
   - The "body of sin" (indwelling sin/sinful nature)
   - The "infirmities of the flesh" (weaknesses and corruptions)

This article sets the foundation for the rest of the Fifth Head, which addresses how true believers, despite their ongoing struggles with sin, are preserved by God's grace and will not finally fall away. It establishes a careful balance: genuine sanctification has truly begun (sin's dominion is broken), yet perfection is not attained in this life — preparing the reader to understand both the reality of believers' falls into sin and God's faithful preservation of them.

questions.response:
The Canons of Dort, produced by the Synod of Dort (1618-1619), address the perseverance of the saints in their Fifth Head of Doctrine. Article 8 of this section teaches that the perseverance of believers is not due to their own merits or strength, but is secured entirely by God's free mercy.

Specifically, Article 8 states that believers do not completely fall from faith and grace, nor do they continue and finally perish in their backslidings, because:

1. **God's counsel cannot be changed** — His eternal purpose of election is unchangeable.

2. **His promise cannot be broken** — God's covenant promises to His people are sure.

3. **The calling according to His purpose cannot be revoked** — Effectual calling is irrevocable.

4. **The merit, intercession, and preservation of Christ cannot be nullified** — Christ's saving work and ongoing intercession secure the believer.

5. **The sealing of the Holy Spirit can neither be frustrated nor destroyed** — The Spirit's work in believers is effective and permanent.

The article emphasizes that perseverance is a work of God's grace from beginning to end, grounded in the Trinitarian work of the Father's election, the Son's mediation, and the Spirit's sealing. This was written largely as a response to the Arminian Remonstrants, who had questioned whether true believers could fall away from grace finally and totally.

The overall thrust is that the security of the believer rests not on human effort or faithfulness but on God's unchangeable character and saving work.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about the holy scriptures?
questions.reference_answer: The Holy Scripture is the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving Knowledge, Faith and Obedience; Although the light of Nature, and the works of Creation and Providence do so far manifest the goodness, wisdom and power of God, as to leave men unexcusable; yet are they not sufficient to give that knowledge of God and His will, which is necessary unto Salvation. Therefore it pleased the Lord at sundry times, and in divers manners, to reveal himself, and to declare that His will unto his Church; and afterward for the better preserving, and propagating of the Truth, and for the more sure Establishment, and Comfort of the Church against the corruption of the flesh, and the malice of Satan, and of the World, to commit the same wholly unto writing; which maketh the Holy Scriptures to be most necessary, those former ways of Gods revealing his will unto his people being now ceased. Under the Name of Holy Scripture or the Word of God written; are now contained all the Books of the Old and New Testament which are these: Of the Old Testament: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, The Song of Songs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi. Of the New Testament: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, The Acts of the Apostles, Pauls Epistle to the Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Phillippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, to Titus, to Philemon, the Epistle to the Hebrews, the Epistle of James, the First and Second Epistles of Peter, the First, Second and Third Epistles of John, the Epistle of Jude, the Revelation. The Books commonly called Apocrypha not being of Divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon (or rule) of the Scripture, and therefore are of no authority to the Church of God, nor to be any otherwise approved or made use of, then other humane writings. The Authority of the Holy Scripture for which it ought to be believed dependeth not upon the testimony of any man, or Church; but wholly upon God (who is truth it self) the Author thereof; therefore it is to be received, because it is the Word of God. We may be moved and induced by the testimony of the Church of God, to an high and reverent esteem of the Holy Scriptures; and the heavenliness of the matter, the efficacy of the Doctrine, and the Majesty of the stile, the consent of all the parts, the scope of the whole (which is to give all glory to God) the full discovery it makes of the only way of mans salvation, and many other incomparable Excellencies, and intire perfections thereof, are arguments whereby it doth abundantly evidence it self to be the Word of God; yet notwithstanding; our full perswasion, and assurance of the infallible truth, and divine authority thereof, is from the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in our Hearts. The whole Councel of God concerning all things necessary for his own Glory, Mans Salvation, Faith and Life, is either expressely set down or necessarily contained in the Holy Scripture; unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new Revelation of the Spirit, or traditions of men.Nevertheless we acknowledge the inward illumination of the Spirit of God, to be necessary for the saving understanding of such things as are revealed in the Word, and that there are some circumstances concerning the worship of God, and government of the Church common to humane actions and societies; which are to be ordered by the light of nature, and Christian prudence according to the general rules of the Word, which are always to be observed. All things in Scripture are not alike plain in themselves, nor alike clear unto all; yet those things which are necessary to be known, believed, and observed for Salvation, are so clearly propounded, and opened in some place of Scripture or other, that not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of ordinary means, may attain to a sufficient understanding of them. The Old Testament in Hebrew, (which was the Native language of the people of God of old) and the New Testament in Greek (which at the time of the writing of it was most generally known to the Nations being immediately inspired by God, and by his singular care and Providence kept pure in all Ages, are therefore authentical; so as in all controversies of Religion the Church is finally to appeal unto them But because these original tongues are not known to all the people of God, who have a right unto, and interest in the Scriptures, and are commanded in the fear of God to read and search them, therefore they are to be translated into the vulgar language of every Nation, unto which they come, that the Word of God dwelling plentifully in all, they may worship him in an acceptable manner, and through patience and comfort of the Scriptures may have hope. The infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture it self: And therefore when there is a question about the true and full sense of any Scripture (which is not manifold but one) it must be searched by other places that speak more clearly. The supream judge by which all controversies of Religion are to be determined, and all Decrees of Councels, opinions of antient Writers, Doctrines of men, and private Spirits, are to be examined, and in whose sentence we are to rest, can be no other but the Holy Scripture delivered by the Spirit, into which Scripture so delivered, our faith is finally resolved.
